executive_summary: GBP/USD closed at 1.3395 on 30 October 2026. The pair is quoted in US dollars per pound, so a rising pair means a stronger pound. It is up 1.52% over one month, down 0.44% over three months and down 1.15% over six, and it sits at the 49th percentile of its 52-week closing range of 1.30152-1.37954. The October rebound from the 14 October intraday low of 1.3138 came as the UK Budget took away the fiscal risk premium and markets moved to price a near-certain Bank of England hike to 4.00% on 5 November. Looked at as a pair, the rates story is flatter than either dossier suggests. The policy gap is only -12.5bp and swings around zero as both central banks hike. Each curve looks over-priced by roughly 50-60bp against its own central bank's projections, so rates net out for this pair. That holds even though the GBP dossier reads BoE over-pricing as sterling-negative and the USD dossier ranks the dollar first of 11 tactically. Energy is what separates the two legs. The UK imports energy and faces a record Q1 2027 gas forward near 238p/therm. The US is a net energy exporter. Over the winter that gap weighs on the pair through the UK external balance and its growth-inflation mix. Tactical (2-4 weeks): Neutral, conviction 2. The weighted score of -0.0992 is a fraction away from Bearish. Dollar funding, BoE communication, energy and event risk lean against the pair. Crowded speculative sterling shorts create squeeze risk the other way. Strategic: Bearish, conviction 2. The score is -0.1738. The three-month base case is 1.3150, inside the six-touch 1.3099-1.3208 support zone. The caveat is that the bearish case rests on one channel. A Hormuz settlement that pulled UK gas forwards below about 160p/therm would remove it quickly. Options already charge for sterling downside, with the six-month 25-delta risk reversal at -0.83 vols.

market_context.valuation_assessment: Both dossiers put GBP/USD fair value on GDP-based PPP at 1.4769, so spot is about 9.3% below PPP. That discount has persisted for years, and neither dossier treats it as actionable inside six months. The real effective exchange rates point the same way. Sterling's BIS real broad index is 111.48, about the 55th percentile of its readings since January 2024, so it is mid-range. The dollar's is 107.11, at the 21st percentile, so the dollar is cheap against its own recent history in trade-weighted terms. Neither leg is stretched. What the current level prices is a structural discount for the UK's 2.5%-of-GDP current account deficit and winter energy bill, offset by near-parity policy rates. Valuation does not limit a move to the low 1.31s, and it does not by itself support a move above 1.37. The pair sits almost exactly mid-range: 4.43 big figures below the closing high and 3.80 above the closing low (intraday range 1.30112-1.38621, 45th percentile).

market_context.recent_regime: GBP/USD fell from a 21 August intraday high of 1.36752 to a 14 October low of 1.31382 as the Fed hiked and gilt stress peaked. It then recovered about 2% in the second half of October as the Budget passed quietly and BoE hike pricing firmed. Spot is now range-bound around flat averages. Sell-side commentary going into the BoE week frames the hike as consensus: ING notes that markets see 'a 25bp rate hike to 4.00% looks like a done deal,' while OCBC warns that with 'plenty of tightening already in the price,' they conclude that 'the bar for the next leg higher in GBP is getting increasingly high.' Energy remains the swing variable. After the 30 October close, oil eased on reports of a 3.5% drop in oil prices, following reports that President Trump wants to give diplomacy with Iran more time. That is a reminder that the Hormuz channel behind the strategic view can move in either direction quickly.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Bank Rate was 3.75% on 26 October and the Fed funds mid-point 3.875% on 27 October, so holding sterling against the dollar costs a negligible 12.5bp a year. Only one scheduled decision falls inside the four-week window: the Bank of England's 5 November meeting, which comes with a Monetary Policy Report. A 25bp hike there would flip the gap to +12.5bp in sterling's favour. But overnight index swaps on 2 November priced a move of about 27bp, so the hike itself is no surprise. The Fed's next decision is 9 December, just after the window, and futures already price a hike at 77-85%, which would hand the dollar back its 12.5bp edge. Two-year gilts at 4.88% on 30 October against 4.61% on Treasuries on 29 October give a 27bp sterling premium that already includes the November move. The tactical question is the path the Monetary Policy Report endorses, not the hike. ING expects a 7-2 vote and calls market pricing for the BoE extreme. Chief Economist Pill has said he is sceptical of four hikes over the next year. With both next moves priced and the gap swinging around zero, the factor is Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months two projection rounds set the differential. The first is the Fed's 9 December decision with its Summary of Economic Projections. The second, at the far edge of the horizon, is the Bank of England's 4 February 2027 Monetary Policy Report, whose date is still provisional; the 17 December BoE meeting has no Report. Each curve looks over-priced against its own central bank. Sterling markets price about 100bp of BoE tightening over a year, to roughly 4.75%, while Oxford Economics sees hikes in November and February to a 4.25% peak and Pill has questioned the priced path. Dollar futures after the 28 October press conference priced the funds rate near 4.7% by September 2027, against a September median dot of 4.1%. If each bank delivers about two fewer hikes than priced, the gap ends near +12.5bp to sterling, close to what pricing already implies. The expected change against the forwards is therefore near zero. The two dossiers disagree on how much Fed tightening is priced, which is the main uncertainty, so we hold Neutral at low confidence and treat the December projections as the first test.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Inflation is running hot in both economies, but the data most likely to surprise sit in different places. The UK has had a run of upside surprises. September CPI was 3.5% against 3.4% expected, with services at 3.7%. The October flash composite PMI hit an eight-month high of 53.1 and unemployment fell to 4.7%. The US has the bigger growth lead, with third-quarter GDP at 3.4% annualised and core PCE at 3.1%, but its labour market is soft: September payrolls rose only 29,000 and earlier months were revised down by 60,000. Inside four weeks the US releases payrolls on 6 November and CPI on 10 November, and the UK releases Q3 GDP on 12 November and labour data on 17 November. The US payroll report can move its central bank's priced path the most. Further UK beats add less because the BoE hike is fully priced, and UK consumer confidence falling 11 points to -24 offsets them. The surprise risks look balanced, so the factor is Neutral.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the mix turns more clearly against sterling. The UK faces an energy-driven inflation peak, with the BoE projecting CPI slightly above 4% in Q1 2027. At the same time the OBR has cut 2027 growth to 1.0%, a stagflationary mix for an economy that imports its energy. The US exports energy on net, so the same shock raises US inflation without the same loss of national income. US growth is expected to slow from 3.4% towards about 2% but to stay above the UK's. The main risk to this stance is the US labour market: three-month average payroll growth is near 51,000 and real wages are falling. UK pay is not spiralling either, with private-sector regular pay at 2.9%, which lets the MPC look through the energy peak after one or two hikes. Relative real growth and the nature of each country's inflation favour the dollar, so the factor is Bearish for the pair at modest confidence.

A prolonged Gulf escalation would instead push the dollar towards the haven side of the smile against energy importers such as the UK. Sterling now trades as a high-yielder rather than a funding currency, so a broad carry unwind would hit it less against the dollar than against the yen or franc. With the two main tails of similar likelihood and the pair's beta modest, the factor carries no signal.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both economies run current account deficits: the UK at 2.5% of GDP and the US at 3.0% in Q2 2026. The energy shock splits them, though. The UK imports energy on net, and its Q1 2027 gas contract made a record close on 28 October, at about 238p per therm on 30 October against an average of about 112p in Q2. The US exports energy on net and its own gas price, Henry Hub at $2.76, is decoupled from European gas. So Brent at $117.64 helps US terms of trade and hurts the UK's. Direct trade is roughly balanced and not a driver. IMF DOTS shows UK exports to the US of $73.7bn and imports of $72.7bn in 2024, a net $1.0bn; US-reported data show a US surplus of about $11.8bn, a mirror difference that does not change the picture. The UK's winter gas bill shows up in trade data from December, but the 12 November trade release can already show whether the August narrowing held. The factor is Bearish at a small tactical weight.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At the strategic weight the external balance is the clearest negative for the pair. Measured against GDP the US deficit is the larger, and its net international investment position worsened by $1.15tn in a quarter to -$22.42tn. But it is financed by strong private inflows, and the energy shock improves US terms of trade. The UK deficit has to absorb a winter gas bill priced off a record Q1 2027 forward, and rising gilt yields are raising payments to foreign investors, which reached £112.9bn in Q2. The UK's services surplus of £51.3bn is a real offset, but it cannot absorb a doubling of gas costs. Over the horizon the energy channel moves the UK balance against sterling faster than the US balance moves against the dollar. The factor is Bearish with the highest confidence of the ten.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: The UK imports energy on net. Oil up and UK wholesale gas (NBP) up are both negative for GBP, with gas the larger channel because it feeds the household price cap and the import bill. Metals and agricultural exposure are minor.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: The US exports energy on net. Oil up is mildly positive for USD through terms of trade and recycled petrodollars. US gas (Henry Hub $2.76) is decoupled from European gas, so a European gas spike does not raise US costs and raises US LNG export income.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Step 1, oil up: GBP negative (energy importer), USD mildly positive (net exporter), so the pair falls. Step 2, European gas up (the direction rule for NBP/TTF): GBP negative, USD unaffected to mildly positive, so the pair falls further. Step 3, gold, iron ore and dairy: no material exposure on either leg. Net: rising energy prices are pair-bearish and falling energy prices pair-bullish, with UK gas the dominant channel because UK wholesale gas has risen faster than oil and passes straight into CPI and the import bill.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Pair-bearish. The UK import bill and CPI rise while US terms of trade improve; the effect is modest on its own and larger if gas moves with oil, as it has during the Gulf conflict.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Pair-bullish. UK real incomes and the current account get relief, at a small cost to US energy income; the effect is largest if the fall reflects a Hormuz settlement that also pulls UK gas forwards lower.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Inside four weeks, communication risk is lopsided against sterling. The Bank of England's 5 November Report will be conditioned on a curve pricing about 100bp of tightening. Pill, one of the hawks, has said he is sceptical of four hikes and that a hike should not suggest a series. ING notes that Governor Bailey has not sounded enthusiastic about hiking, and two members, Dhingra and Taylor, are firmly opposed. A hike that comes with projections showing inflation at or below target on market rates would be a 'dovish hike'. On the dollar side, the Fed's statement of 28 October was hawkish, with two governors voting for an immediate hike. The minutes due on 18 November could reveal support for a hike beyond those two dissents. Chair Warsh gives no forward guidance, so Fed communication in the window comes mainly from the minutes. The skew favours a cautious BoE message against a hawkish Fed record, so the factor is Bearish at low confidence.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months both central banks are credible, and both face curves priced beyond their own projections. The Fed's 9 December projections, the first under a chair who gives no forward guidance, can confirm the 4.1% median dot against market pricing near 4.7% for late 2027. That would be dollar-negative. The BoE's next Report, provisionally dated 4 February 2027, can confirm a 4.25% peak against about 4.75% priced, which would be sterling-negative. Both banks publish votes, so any shift in the hawkish wing will be visible quickly. Because both curves are likely to be pushed back by credible central banks with similar gaps, the factor is Neutral strategically.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The 3 November US midterms are largely priced, with a Democratic House the overwhelming expectation. A change of House control could revive trade policy, which ING sees as dollar-negative. The bigger event is the Iran war. The White House has said it would not strike Iran before the midterms, which leaves the weeks after 3 November open, and two tankers were hit in the Strait of Hormuz on 29-30 October. Escalation would hurt sterling through energy far more than the dollar, because the US is a net energy exporter. A settlement would do the reverse. The dossiers put escalation within four weeks at 20-30% against 10-15% for a settlement, which tilts the distribution against the pair. The UK's main domestic event, the 28 October Budget, has passed without stress. The factor is Bearish at low confidence.

On the UK side, the new government's fiscal room is thin before the spring tests. A winter Gulf escalation would hit an energy-importing economy whose Q1 gas contract is already at a record. The energy tail is the larger and more likely of these shocks and falls mainly on the base currency. That offsets the US political calendar and leaves the factor mildly Bearish.

The US deficit is the larger, at 6.2% of GDP in FY2026, with interest costs at 3.4% of GDP. With no fiscal trigger on either side in four weeks, the factor is Neutral.

tactical.score_interpretation: A net score of -0.0992 sits just inside the Neutral band, a fraction of a point from Bearish. Four factors lean against the pair: USD liquidity (-0.056), guidance (-0.037), external balance (-0.033) and event risk (-0.026). One leans for it: positioning (+0.053). The other five are Neutral, including the heaviest, Policy & Rates. The tilt comes from breadth, not depth: no factor carries more than 55% confidence, and the largest single contribution is the short-covering risk that works in the pair's favour. -0.0992 falls inside the ±0.10 Neutral band, so the stance is Neutral at conviction 2. The score sits 0.0008 inside the band, so a one-point change in confidence on any Bearish factor would flip the label. We read this as a Neutral with a bearish lean for risk management: it is a reason not to fade the pair from above the 200-day average, and not a reason to buy it.
tactical.rationale: At tactical weights Policy & Rates (0.24), Inflation & Growth (0.18) and USD Liquidity (0.11) carry over half the score, and the first two are Neutral. That is why the result is a borderline -0.099 rather than a clear call. Policy is Neutral because both next moves are priced: a BoE hike on 5 November and a Fed hike on 9 December, which leaves the gap swinging around zero. Inflation & Growth is Neutral because UK upside surprises and a softening US labour market cancel at this horizon. The bearish lean comes from four smaller factors. Dollar funding is tightening into month-end. The BoE's 5 November Report is more likely to push back on the 100bp priced than the Fed minutes on 18 November are to sound dovish. An energy-importing UK faces a record winter gas forward. And the post-midterm Iran window would hit sterling harder than the dollar. Against that, speculators are short sterling and long dollars, so a hawkish Report or a weak 6 November US payroll print could force a squeeze. The two dossiers mostly offset here: the GBP dossier is Neutral on sterling and the USD dossier Bullish on the dollar, but the dollar's tactical strength is concentrated against the euro, yen and franc, not sterling. What is priced is a near-certain BoE hike. Our edge, if any, is the risk that the Report reads as a 'dovish hike', which is modest. The path of least resistance is two-way trading around the 5 November decision, with the US payroll report on 6 November, US CPI on 10 November, UK Q3 GDP on 12 November and UK labour data on 17 November as the dated tests. Conviction is 2, not 1, because the factors genuinely offset rather than being absent and the catalysts are dense. It is not higher because the score sits at the band's edge and the largest contributor works against the lean. Levels for any expression are set in the trade plan.
tactical.g10_relative_ranking: Tactically GBP/USD is a weak way to express the dollar view. The USD dossier ranks the dollar 1st of 11 and the GBP dossier ranks sterling 5th, so dollar strength is better expressed against the euro, franc or yen, where policy gaps of 137.5-387.5bp and weaker terms of trade do the work. Among sterling crosses, short EUR/GBP has the clearer tactical edge on the BoE-ECB gap. GBP/USD ranks near the bottom of the dollar-long opportunity set this month.

strategic.score_interpretation: A net score of -0.174 is Bearish but shallow. Three factors carry it: External Balance (-0.093), Inflation & Growth (-0.055) and Event Risk (-0.026). The other seven are Neutral and none is Bullish. The call rests mainly on one channel, the energy shock: it hits the UK's external balance and inflation mix while improving US terms of trade. Policy & Rates, the heaviest factor, adds nothing because both curves look over-priced by similar amounts. -0.1738 is beyond the -0.10 threshold, so the stance is Bearish at conviction 2.
strategic.rationale: At strategic weights Policy & Rates (0.24), External Balance (0.16), Guidance (0.12) and USD Liquidity (0.12) dominate, and only External Balance gives a clear signal, which makes it the main driver of the -0.17 score. The core of the view is that the energy shock divides the two economies. The UK imports energy on net and faces a Q1 2027 gas forward near 238p per therm, more than double the Q2 average, which will weigh on a 2.5%-of-GDP current account deficit through the winter. The US exports energy on net and gains terms of trade from Brent near $118. The same shock turns UK growth and inflation into a stagflationary mix, with 2027 growth of 1.0% and CPI above 4% in Q1, while US growth slows but stays ahead. The dossiers conflict on rates. The GBP dossier sees an over-priced BoE as the main bearish channel. The USD dossier sees an equally over-priced Fed path, near 4.7% against a 4.1% median dot. Taken together the relative repricing nets out, so we score Policy and Guidance Neutral rather than letting either dossier's framing dominate. What is priced is an unchanged differential with both banks still hiking. Our edge is the external and growth divergence, which forwards with negligible carry do not price. The path of least resistance is lower through the winter gas season. The 9 December Fed projections are the first test: confirmation of a single further hike would weaken the dollar leg and challenge this view. The 17 December BoE decision and the provisional 4 February 2027 Report test the sterling leg. Conviction is held at 2 rather than 3 for three reasons: the score is shallow, it depends on one channel, and a Hormuz settlement would reverse that channel quickly. Levels for any expression are set in the trade plan.

The dollar screens as the stronger leg against only five currencies (AUD, CAD, NZD, GBP, EUR), so short GBP/USD is one of the few majors where the dollar leg is favoured, second only to short EUR/USD. Among sterling shorts, GBP/NOK and GBP/CAD capture the energy channel more directly and with positive carry for the short, so they rank ahead of GBP/USD as pure energy expressions.

consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: Cannot be measured against a bank consensus because none was located. Qualitatively, the view is below (less constructive than) published sterling commentary that has upgraded the pound on the BoE's hawkish turn.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Not quantified against a bank-survey median, as none was found. For context only: our 1.3150 three-month base case sits about 210 pips below the aggregated Q4 2026 sentiment-survey consensus of 1.3358 (26 providers, range 1.2700-1.4000); it is close to a broker January path of 1.3127 and above Goldman Sachs' six-month 1.29. Named calls bracket the view: Goldman Sachs 1.33 in three months and 1.29 in six; UBS 1.38 and Bank of America 1.37 for end-2026; MUFG 1.31 at year-end. A Reuters survey found only about half of respondents expecting another BoE increase in Q1 2027.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: Published commentary has upgraded sterling on the BoE's turn, much of it against the euro, where a 125bp rate advantage and French political stress flatter the pound. Against the dollar the policy gap is near zero and both curves look over-priced by similar amounts, so rates give sterling no relative edge. We weigh the energy channel more heavily than commentary does. It hits a UK that imports energy through its current account and real incomes, while improving US terms of trade, and UK trade data will show the winter gas bill only from December.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: If the external and growth divergence asserts itself through the winter, the pair falls with negligible carry cost, because forwards price almost no change.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: A Hormuz settlement that pulls UK gas forwards sharply lower, or a December Fed projection round that confirms one final hike while the BoE validates a second, would remove the energy channel or shift the rate channel in sterling's favour. Crowded speculative sterling shorts would speed up that reversal.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The horizons share a bearish lean but land on opposite sides of the threshold. Tactically, priced moves from both central banks, balanced data risk and crowded speculative shorts hold the score at -0.099. Strategically, the weight shifts towards External Balance (0.16), where the energy shock divides the two economies, and Inflation & Growth turns Bearish as UK stagflation takes hold, giving -0.174.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The 9 December FOMC decision with projections, and then the 17 December BoE decision, are the first points where the strategic divergence can be confirmed or challenged. The BoE's 4 February 2027 Report (provisional) is the later sterling-side test.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Treat the tactical window around the 5 November BoE decision as two-way risk, with squeeze potential from speculative shorts. The strategic bearish view is better expressed after that event risk has cleared than ahead of it. Tactical: run only the range legs between 1.3240 and 1.3590 during November. Strategic: build the short through Entry A on any post-Report rally into 1.3480-1.3550, or Entry B on a daily close below 1.3236, and size both at conviction-2 risk.

catalysts.rationale: A Democratic House is widely expected, and a change of control could revive trade policy, which ING sees as dollar-negative. The result also opens the window in which US strikes on Iran become possible, which would hit sterling through energy harder than the dollar.

Coupon sizes are expected to stay unchanged. Any weakening of the pledge to hold them would lift US term premia. In this regime that weighs on the dollar through fiscal concern rather than supporting it through yield, and it would favour the pair.

catalysts.event: Bank of England decision with Monetary Policy Report
catalysts.rationale: A hike to 4.00% is fully priced and would briefly put Bank Rate 12.5bp above the Fed mid-point. The pair's reaction depends on the vote split and the conditioned projections. A 7-2 hike with inflation at target on market rates would be a 'dovish hike' and pair-negative; an endorsement of further tightening would trigger short-covering. Commentary frames the vote split as the risk: the key question is whether the Bank signals more increases to come or hints that it is prepared to pause. A hawkish steer would offer the pound some support, while a more cautious message could leave sterling exposed.

Consensus is about +55,000 after a 29,000 September gain and downward revisions. A print near zero would cut December Fed pricing and, with speculators long dollars and short sterling, could squeeze the pair higher. A strong print would lock in the Fed hike.

September core CPI rose 0.3% month on month with a 3.4% three-month annualised pace. A repeat keeps the Fed hiking alongside the BoE and leaves the bilateral differential unchanged; a soft print would weaken the dollar leg.

catalysts.event: UK Q3 GDP preliminary estimate, September GDP and trade
catalysts.rationale: A Q3 print above the BoE's 0.4% estimate would support a second hike in February, which is pair-positive. The trade data show whether the August narrowing held as energy prices rose, an early read on the external channel behind the strategic view.

catalysts.event: UK labour market release (three months to September)
catalysts.rationale: Unemployment fell to 4.7%, with regular pay at 3.7%. A rebound in joblessness would undercut the case for more BoE hikes and confirm the consumer squeeze; pay above 3.8% would support the priced path and the pair.

The minutes will show how many participants beyond the two dissenters favoured a hike. Broader hawkish support would firm December pricing and the dollar's rate edge after the BoE's November move, weighing on the pair.

catalysts.event: Ofgem announcement of the January 2027 household energy price cap (fourth week of November)
catalysts.rationale: The cap passes the record Q1 2027 gas forward, near 238p/therm, to UK households from January, adding to CPI and squeezing real incomes. That is the Factor 2 and Factor 5 channel, and it has no US counterpart because Henry Hub gas is decoupled. A large rise confirms the strategic stagflation mix.

catalysts.event: FOMC decision with Summary of Economic Projections
catalysts.rationale: A hike to 4.00-4.25% is mostly priced and would restore a 12.5bp dollar edge over a 4.00% Bank Rate. The projections decide whether the market's roughly 4.7% path for 2027 survives. A single-hike-and-hold signal would weaken the dollar leg and challenge the strategic bearish view.

catalysts.event: Expiry of the US government's continuing resolution
catalysts.rationale: The stopgap signed on 2 September expires on 11 December. A funding lapse would delay US data and raise the fiscal risk premium on US assets, which in this regime weakens the dollar and would support the pair.

catalysts.event: Bank of England decision (no Monetary Policy Report)
catalysts.rationale: A hold after a November hike is the likely outcome. The vote split will show whether a February move has support, and fewer hawks would confirm the strategic case for a short cycle. It comes a week after the Fed, so it responds to the December projections.

catalysts.event: UK Q3 2026 balance of payments (fourth week of December)
catalysts.rationale: The first quarterly current account reading to include the autumn energy run-up. A deficit wider than Q2's 2.5% of GDP, with primary income payments still rising on higher gilt yields, would confirm Factor 5 at its 0.16 strategic weight.

catalysts.event: Bank of England decision with Monetary Policy Report (provisional date)
catalysts.rationale: The Bank has published this date but not committed to it. The Report will be conditioned on whatever the curve prices. If it shows the Committee comfortable at 4.25%, the 2027 sterling strip reprices lower, which is pair-negative; validation of further hikes would be pair-positive.

invalidators.condition: The MPC hikes on 5 November by 9-0 or 8-1 with guidance endorsing further tightening, and the two-year gilt-Treasury spread widens above +50bp within a week
invalidators.mechanism: The 'dovish hike' risk behind Factor 6 would reverse, and a crowded short in both legs (sterling legacy net -79,400, dollar longs about $15.9bn) would be forced to cover with no carry cushion.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: MPC vote split and 2Y gilt minus 2Y Treasury (currently +27bp)

invalidators.condition: The UK Q1 2027 gas forward falls below 160p/therm for 10 consecutive sessions, most likely on a Hormuz framework
invalidators.mechanism: The energy channel that carries Factor 5 (-0.093) and Factor 2 (-0.055) is the only source of the strategic Bearish score. Without it, the remaining Event Risk contribution alone sits inside the Neutral band.

invalidators.condition: The 9 December FOMC projections show no further hike in 2027 (median 2027 dot at or below 4.0%) while the 17 December BoE minutes record three or more votes for a further hike
invalidators.mechanism: The rate repricing would no longer net out: the dollar curve would lose 50-70bp of priced tightening against a sterling curve that holds, moving Factor 1 in sterling's favour.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: FOMC dot plot and BoE vote

invalidators.condition: The UK Q3 current account (due late December) shows a deficit narrowing below 2.0% of GDP while gas forwards stay above 200p/therm
invalidators.mechanism: That would show the UK services surplus absorbing the energy bill, removing the pair-specific external divergence.

invalidators.condition: US October and November payrolls are both negative with unemployment at 4.4% or higher
invalidators.new_stance: Tactical stance turns Bullish and strategic stance turns Neutral
invalidators.mechanism: December Fed pricing would fall below 40%, the USD liquidity headwind (Factor 10) would fade as the Fed signals a peak, and dollar-side hedging flows would offset UK structural hedging.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: US payrolls and December hike probability (currently 77.3%)

invalidators.condition: GBP/USD closes a week above 1.3640, above the top of the five-touch resistance zone
invalidators.new_stance: Strategic short stopped out; view turns Neutral unless the gas forward remains above 200p/therm and the Fed's December projections have not shown a hold
invalidators.mechanism: A sustained break would mean one of the conditions in invalidators 1-5 is already under way.
invalidators.monitor_indicator: Weekly close against 1.3640, alongside the gas forward

assumptions: Price series: the price data are daily closing prices for 130 weekday sessions from 2026-05-04 to 2026-10-30. Spot is 1.3395 at the 30 October close. Moving averages and support and resistance zones are computed over the full stored history of 4,957 weekday sessions from 2007-10-09 to 2026-10-30, which includes 1,011 weekly and 502 monthly bars. The series contains no weekend bars, so every window is a true trading-day window.

Spot date: the 30 October close falls two calendar days before the 1 November valuation date, which is a weekend, so no trading sessions are missing. Every level, pip distance and percentage in this report is computed against 1.3395. Later web quotes have not been substituted.
Price-derived figures: all averages are simple averages of trading-day closes. Realised volatility is annualised on 252 trading days. ATR(14) is 75 pips.

Zones: distances are quoted to each zone's midpoint, with the near edge stated separately. Zones are ranked by touch count, the number of weekly or monthly swing closes that formed them. Narrative range positioning uses the closing-basis 52-week percentile (49th); the intraday-basis percentile is the 45th.

What the factor stances rest on: no trailing returns, moving averages, ranges or support and resistance levels were used in any factor stance. The only exception is Factor 9, whose subject is how the pair itself trades. Price data were used for entries, targets, stops, sizing, invalidator levels, scenarios and the market-context narrative.

Policy rates and yields: Bank Rate is 3.75% as of 26 October and the Fed funds mid-point 3.875% as of 27 October. The 10-year differential of +25bp uses September monthly averages (5.24% vs 4.99%) and is not a live level. Daily two-year and 10-year yields are taken from the dossiers with their observation dates.

Options: implied volatility, risk reversals and butterflies are CME at-the-money quotes on British pound futures options observed 29 October. The three-month tenor is measured at 98.7 days, not 90, because CME lists quarterly expiries. The GBP dossier's readings from one day earlier (one-month 6.04%) differ slightly and are not used. A full-year implied-volatility percentile is not available (iv_percentile is therefore null), and no public option-barrier data for this pair was located.

Forward points: the 9.8bp annualised premium between the November and December 2026 CME sterling futures, observed 29 October, contains both the interest differential and any cross-currency basis, which cannot be separated without an OIS curve. Forward points are derived from it. The GBP dossier's 0.0bp reading from 28 October is not used.

Dossier conflicts: the two dossiers disagree on some figures: UK CPI (3.5% vs 3.3%), the UK current account (-2.5% vs -2.84% of GDP) and how much Fed tightening is priced. The GBP dossier's UK figures are used, and the Fed-pricing conflict is treated as uncertainty in Factor 1. The 200-week average from the price data (1.29369) supersedes the GBP dossier's 1.29303.

Meeting schedule: the BoE meets on 5 November (with Report), 17 December and 4 February 2027 (with Report, provisional). The FOMC meets on 9 December (with projections). No FOMC decision is placed between 9 December and 1 March 2027.

Forecasts: no formal bank-survey median for GBP/USD exists. Named bank forecasts and aggregator consensus are reported for context only and are not treated as a survey consensus, so bank_consensus_forecast is null.

Bilateral trade: bilateral goods trade is IMF DOTS 2024 data: UK exports to the US $73.7bn, imports $72.7bn, net +$1.0bn. US-reported mirror data show US exports to the UK of $79.9bn and imports of $68.1bn. Both show broadly balanced flows.
Probabilities: event probabilities for Iran escalation and settlement are the dossiers' estimates, quoted as ranges where they differ. Scenario and invalidator probabilities are our own estimates.

Weights and horizons: default factor weights are applied with no pair-specific adjustments. The tactical horizon is four weeks. Strategic factor assessments look one to three months ahead; scenarios target 5 February 2027, and the forward table extends to six months.

Date formatting: the source report dated two catalysts by week only (Ofgem January cap in the fourth week of November; UK Q3 balance of payments in the fourth week of December). They are entered as 2026-11-23 and 2026-12-22 respectively to satisfy the date format; the exact release dates are not stated in the report. Dossier dates in metadata are set to the valuation date as the report does not state them separately.

Positioning percentile fields: base_cftc_percentile uses the sterling three-year COT index reading of 11 and quote_cftc_percentile uses the 83rd one-year percentile of ICE dollar-index non-commercial length, as stated in the report.
